cooktopSubstrates.name: Lithium Aluminosilicate (LAS) Glass-Ceramic (Schott Ceran / EuroKera)
cooktopSubstrates.description: Standard high-performance glass-ceramic engineered with near-zero thermal expansion coefficient. Extremely resistant to pure thermal shock, but brittle and vulnerable to localized Hertzian point impacts and quartz abrasion.

cooktopSubstrates.name: Standard Vitroceramic (Radiant / Halogen Element Top)
cooktopSubstrates.description: Formulated for radiant coiled ribbon burners. Subjected to extreme underside operational temperatures (up to 550°C top / 900°C underside), creating substantial radial hoop stresses between active zones and cold glass borders.

cooktopSubstrates.name: Optimized Induction Cold-Glass Substrate
cooktopSubstrates.description: Used on modern electromagnetic induction cooktops. Because glass is only heated by conductive back-transfer from cookware (rarely exceeding 200°C), thermal degradation and sugar caramelization spalling risks are reduced by 70%.

cooktopSubstrates.name: Tempered Soda-Lime Glass (Budget Cooktops / Splash Insets)
cooktopSubstrates.description: Standard thermally toughened float glass with high compressive surface layer. Highly susceptible to thermal shock failure (>160°C delta) and shatters catastrophically into thousands of granular dice if compressive layer is breached.

cooktopSubstrates.name: Borosilicate Low-Expansion Glass
cooktopSubstrates.description: Low thermal expansion glass with good chemical resistance. Lower mechanical flexural strength and toughness than ceramic glass, prone to chipping under point impact.

abrasionHazards.name: Pristine Smooth Pan Base / No Abrasion
abrasionHazards.description: Smooth aluminum or buffed copper pan base with zero particulate debris.

abrasionHazards.name: Smooth 304 Stainless Steel Pan Base (Clean)
abrasionHazards.description: Clean stainless steel cookware. Minimal scratch formation unless pushed under heavy force.

abrasionHazards.name: Rough Raw Cast Iron Base (Casting Nodules & Burrs)
abrasionHazards.description: Sand-cast iron with microscopic surface spikes and iron carbide ($Fe_3C$) inclusions that gouge glass-ceramic when dragged.

abrasionHazards.name: Unglazed Ceramic Casserole / Stoneware Foot Ring
abrasionHazards.description: Unglazed vitrified stoneware bottom rim has Mohs hardness 7.0, harder than glass-ceramic. Generates micro-chipping and linear surface scoring.

abrasionHazards.name: Quartz Sand / Mineral Grit Trapped Under Heavy Pan (Mohs 7.0)
abrasionHazards.description: Windblown dirt, unwashed potato sand, or coarse mineral grit. Point pressure from heavy pan crushes quartz into glass, producing severe crack-initiating notches.

chemicalHazards.name: Clean Surface / No Chemical Contaminant
chemicalHazards.description: Clean glass surface with standard dry cooking environment.

chemicalHazards.name: Starchy Pasta Water Boilover
chemicalHazards.description: Deposition of gelatinized amylose and mineral salts. Leaves chalky ring but minimal tensile bond.

chemicalHazards.name: Acidic Tomato Marinara Boilover (pH 4.1)
chemicalHazards.description: Weak acidic etching combined with moderate fructose adhesion. Easily cleaned if wiped while warm.

chemicalHazards.name: Melted Cheese / Burnt Milk Soil
chemicalHazards.description: Charred proteins and milk sugars adhere tightly to the glass silicate matrix. Requires specialized scraper.

chemicalHazards.name: Boiling High-Sugar Caramel / Fruit Jam (Spalling Hazard)
chemicalHazards.description: Molten sucrose (160°C+) creates direct chemical bonds with silicate ions. As it cools, differential thermal contraction exerts immense shear, pulling micro-chips of glass straight out of the surface.

emergencySafetyProtocols.title: Immediate Power Isolation at Main Breaker Panel
emergencySafetyProtocols.action: Do not attempt to touch switches on the cooktop if surface is cracked. Go to your home's main electrical breaker panel and flip off the dedicated 240V double-pole circuit breaker (typically 30–50 Amps) for the range/cooktop.
emergencySafetyProtocols.rationale: High-voltage 240V live terminal blocks and heating coils sit just 4–8 millimeters below the ceramic glass. Liquid spills through a crack can energize the entire wet countertop, creating a lethal electrocution and arc flash hazard.

emergencySafetyProtocols.title: Immediate Sugar Spill Razor Scraper Protocol
emergencySafetyProtocols.action: If molten caramel, jam, or granulated sugar spills on a hot burner, NEVER let it cool down! Put on a heat-resistant oven mitt, take a single-edge razor blade scraper held at a 30-degree angle, and immediately shave the hot liquid sugar off the burner zone into a cool metal spatula or damp cloth.
emergencySafetyProtocols.rationale: Once sugar drops below 100°C, it crosslinks to the silica matrix and contracts with tremendous tensile force, ripping permanent pits out of the glass surface during cooling.

emergencySafetyProtocols.title: Never Use Pot Protectors or Heat Diffuser Mats with Radiant Cooktops
emergencySafetyProtocols.action: Do not place silicone liners, fiberglass mats, or metallic heat diffuser disks on radiant glass-ceramic cooktops.
emergencySafetyProtocols.rationale: While silicone mats are marketed for induction cooktops (which stay relatively cool), placing a silicone mat on a radiant cooktop (400°C+) results in immediate silicone pyrolysis, melting fluoropolymers and fusing permanently to the glass.

emergencySafetyProtocols.title: Cast Iron Lift-and-Place Rule
emergencySafetyProtocols.action: Always lift cast iron, stoneware, and enameled Dutch ovens straight up rather than sliding or nudging them across burner zones. Periodically inspect the bottom of all cookware with your fingers for rough burrs or sand grit.
emergencySafetyProtocols.rationale: Sliding under heavy vertical downward load creates microscopic Griffith flaw notches that halve the flexural impact strength of the cooktop over time.
